newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia leaders talk up markets, not economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia leaders talk up markets, not economy.

text.p: Malaysian leaders have again "talked up" the country's financial markets, but many dealers and analysts said on Thursday they remained confused over the direction of the fast-growing economy.

Remarks by Prime Minister Mahathir and his deputy and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim over the ringgit and planned reviews of major infrastructure projects pushed up the local currency and the stock market.
The ringgit fell back after an initial rise when Indonesia's central bank scrapped the rupiah's intervention band system.
Stock prices, on a recovery since Wednesday after days of sharp falls, continued to rise on Thursday.

Mahathir said late on Wednesday that Malaysia would reduce its imports by reviewing implementation of some large infrastructure projects to keep the current account deficit in check after the ringgit's fall. The currency has declined nearly 11 percent against the U.S. dollar in the past month.
"Now our import cost is a little bit more because the value of ringgit has come down. For the time being, we have got to reduce imports but we will go on with these projects," he said.

Anwar on Thursday hinted at possible tax and fiscal measures in next year's budget to curb imports. He said on Tuesday that implementation of some "mega-projects" not considered "critical" for the economy will be postponed if required.
"What the leaders are doing is talking up the markets. If you look closely, there does not seem (to be) much clarity on the policy front," said an economist with a Malaysian research house.
"The leaders have been contradicting each other. While one is saying projects will be deferred, the other says they will not be," said the analyst, who declining to be identified.
Anwar said on Thursday that some projects, like ports development, need not be deferred.
"Anwar has in the past been a strong advocate that projects be deferred, but the PM has been asking to go ahead full steam with projects," the economist said.
Mahathir has set 2020 as the target by which Malaysia should become a fully developed nation, something that economists have said requires maintaining more than eight percent annual growth.
The two leaders did not say which projects were under review. Analysts said such information would be crucial in determining if Malaysia was serious in its attempts to slow down the economy.
"The government is confusing people by saying too many things," said a dealer at a Malaysian brokerage. "There should be clarity when the markets are so volatile."
An economist with a Malaysian brokerage said: "There is a degree of incoherence. This was the issue in the 1996 budget too, when they made promises which they have not really kept.
"In 1996, they cut imports of items like aircraft and ships, but did not slow down on growth-oriented projects," he said.
Last year, Malaysia cut economic growth to 8.2 percent from a peak of 9.5 percent in 1995, and the current account deficit to five percent of gross domestic product from more than eight percent.
Economists have said the Malaysian economy, after averaging eight percent growth for a decade, was showing signs of strain.

"Malaysia is entering a period of structural adjustment. The period of high growth has led to some negative factors like a tight labour market and too much property being built," said Daniel Lian, regional economist with NatWest Markets.

The latest round of fears over the Malaysian economy are being expressed in the wake of the ringgit's fall, a whopping 2.8 billion ringgit trade deficit for June and high loan growth of 30 percent year-on-year in June.

"The supply and demand side equation is not exactly balanced (in Malaysia). I think growth is very strong, in fact too strong," said Chia Woon Khien, economist with Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in Singapore.
